newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal-hit firms cut off some sokaiya funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal-hit firms cut off some sokaiya funds.

text.p: Two top Japanese financial firms have taken symbolic steps to break their ties to racketeers by cutting off a key source of funds for the corporate extortionists who have ensnared them in a big payoff scandal.
But the decades-old symbiosis between companies and corporate extortionists is unlikely to disappear quickly, even if other companies are persuaded to follow suit.
Nomura Securities said on Thursday that it would cancel subscriptions to hundreds of periodicals, many of which financial experts say are really tools for extortion.

A spokesman for the giant brokerage said Nomura would notify publishers of some 700 periodicals, newspapers and newsletters that it was cancelling its subscriptions and would resume only those deemed "appropriate".
Cancelling subscriptions might seem an odd way for the brokerage -- now embroiled in a huge scandal over payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer -- to clean up its act.

But forcing firms to buy their publications or risk public exposure of dubious practices has been a key tactic used by sokaiya to extort money from companies, especially after direct payoffs were banned in 1983, financial experts say.

Prosecutors on Wednesday charged Nomura with violating securities law and indicted its former president, Hideo Sakamaki, and a former managing director for conspiring to pay 320 million yen ($2.83 million) in cash to Ryuichi Koike, the sokaiya at the heart of the scandal. It was the second indictment in the case for both Nomura and Sakamaki.

The affair has also led to the arrest of 11 officials from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), one of the nation's biggest banks. A former DKB chairman committed suicide last month after being questioned about his role in arranging allegedly illegal loans by the bank to Koike.
A DKB spokesman said the bank had also cancelled periodical subscriptions by its general affairs department, traditionally the corporate section responsible for coping with sokaiya.

Sokaiya, often linked to "yakuza" crime syndicates, typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices in their publications or by raising embarrassing questions at shareholders meetings.
The racketeers have also been known to threaten bodily harm to corporate executives and industry sources complain police action is often too little and too late.
In one well-publicised case, police blamed a sokaiya for the 1994 murder of a Fuji Photo official.

Companies in the past have also hired sokaiya to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions at annual shareholders' gatherings, a practice critics say stems from a deep-rooted corporate allergy to disclosure and disdain for investors.

The moves by Nomura and DKB mirror that by department store Takashimaya Co Ltd, which last year cancelled about 300 periodical subscriptions as part of its effort to cut links to racketeers and other "anti-social groups".
The prestigious retailer suffered a major blow to its image last June after police arrested two senior officials of the company on suspicion of paying off sokaiya.

"We had a reaction from some groups, who urged us not to cancel, but we checked the appropriateness of the publications in consultation with police and lawyers and if they were inappropriate, we cancelled them," a spokeswoman told Reuters.
But whether many other firms will follow suit is unclear.

A spokesman for Daiwa Securities Co Ltd declined comment on the subject, while spokesmen for the other two of Japan's Big Four brokerages -- Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd -- said the matter was "under consideration."
Pressure to unravel corporate ties to sokaiya is mounting as Japan implements drastic reforms to bring its financial industry up to global standards.

Authorities are talking tough, but sceptics say the outcome is hardly assured. "There are a couple of thousand of the guys (sokaiya) out there, and they are hardly going to become sushi chefs overnight," one legal source said. ($1=113 yen)
